title: How do we make a thirty degree angle by cutting sixty in half?
description: A sixty degree angle from an equilateral triangle, then two arcs of one radius that meet inside it. The line to their meeting point makes two matching triangles, so it cuts the sixty into two equal angles. Keeko's doubt, arcs of different radii, is struck.
teaching_notes: One idea: equal arcs from the two arms give two triangles that match side side side, so the line cuts the angle in half. Watch for students who change the compass opening between the two arcs.

source: Construct a 30° angle at a point A on a line, using only a r
video_script.why: The child sees that cutting a sixty degree angle in half gives an exact thirty degree angle, and why the cut is fair.
video_script.substitution: One compass opening is used for both bisecting arcs, so BD equals CD.
video_script.anchor: A line with the point A marked on it, a ruler and a compass.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko draws the arcs from B and from C with different radii. Then BD and CD are not equal, the two triangles do not match, and AD does not cut the angle in half.
video_script.payoff_line: Angle D eigh B is thirty degrees.

final_answer.spoken: angle D eigh B is thirty degrees

maths_rules: Centre A, any radius, cut the line at B. Centre B, same radius, cut the arc at C. Triangle ABC is equilateral, so ∠CAB = 60°.
Bisect ∠CAB: arcs from B and from C with one radius meet at D inside the angle. Join A and D.
AB = AC (radii of one arc), BD = CD (one radius), AD is common, so triangle ABD is congruent to triangle ACD by SSS.
So ∠DAB = ∠DAC, and each is half of 60°, which is 30°.
Slip: arcs of different radii make BD unequal to CD, so the triangles do not match.
video_script.design: One line, one point A, a sixty degree angle and two more arcs. The two triangles are shaded in two colours so the match shows. The slip is two different radii.
